posts.name: Dalyodh Singh
posts.cooked: @sayan can you please explain why it is not ideal to make permissions 777

posts.name: Sayan Ghosh
posts.cooked:
As mentioned in the original post’s moderation, 777 means read, write, and execute permission for current user, current group, and all other users.

Letting anyone and everyone have write access (and in most cases even read access) to your files is not secure.

This is a bad practice of simply slapping 777 without understanding the implications of it. It also does not follow the principle of least privilege refer here.

Only give permissions you need to give. If you are writing a script and need to run it, give it executable permission for your user only. u+x.

posts.cooked:
got it bro thanks you
but can you explain me any situation here in the case of script.sh in my vm how others can make changes and

  • what effect it will make if I gave executive permission t o other and group
  • what effect it will make if i give only read and right permission to other and group

I am asking this for only curiosity ,please tell me what should i put instead ? chmod 746 or chmod 764 and tell me consequences of it in details

I will be very helpful for me.
Regards,
Dalyodh Singh

posts.name: Sayan Ghosh
posts.cooked:
User permissions applies on only the owner of the file, no one else.
Group permissions applies on all members of the group which owns the file.
Anyone permissions applies to the rest.

If you are creating a script for yourself you do not need to provide any permissions to others, so it can even be 700. In fact, the .ssh/id_rsa{,.pub} files are supposed to have a 600 permission so other users or groups cannot even read it.

If you are working collaboratively and want others in the group to also be able to edit it, you can give read and write permission to the group -6-.

If you really want everyone to be able to read some file, give it 4, if you also want them to be able to write it, give 6, if they should be allowed to execute, give 7.

This is basic permissions, there are also things like sticky bit and set-uid and set-gid, which are explained in details in the book, please refer those for more details.

posts.name: Sayan Ghosh
posts.cooked:
If you give 777, it wont directly have an effect as your parent directories have the correct permissions, however if those were changed too, then you basically are allowing all other students to see and make changes to your scripts.

My post is on a more generic note, so as to inculcate the idea that having broader permissions is a security risk.

Instead of 777 you can put 764. You do not have to explicitly mention the other permissions if you just want to add executable permissions for the user, just simply use chmod u+x instead.
